rationale: The book's core identification — that 'works' names deeds as such, and that a deed's status as obedience or disobedience is a relational property determined by whose command it executes — is directly carried by the printed texts. Exodus 18:20 introduces 'the work that they must do' alongside ordinances taught and a way walked, treating work as the deed distinct from the command. Micah 6:16 shows the same grammar on the evil side: the 'works of the house of Ahab' are deeds executing 'the statutes of Omri' — evil works are command-executing deeds whose master is illegitimate, exactly the book's mechanism. Psalm 111:7 pairs God's works with His commandments; Revelation 2:26 ('keepeth my works') confirms works are commandment-shaped and keepable. Luke 17:7-10 supplies the decisive wage distinction: even complete obedience creates no wage-claim, which cleanly separates the Romans 4 laborer ('reward... of debt') from obedience per se, and reconciles Romans 4:4-5 with Hebrews 11:8 ('by faith Abraham obeyed') and James 2:21-22 without setting faith against obedience. No specific counter-reading I can formulate explains this text-set — especially the Micah/Exodus command-relative usage and the Luke 17 duty-without-wage saying — with fewer unsupported steps. The common evidential-fruit interpretation shares the book's core referent (works = deeds) and is not a rival identification; the genuinely rival reading (works as intrinsically meaning self-justifying moral effort, so that Paul opposes faith to obedience as such) handles Romans 4 by importing a meaning that Psalm 111:7, Micah 6:16, Revelation 2:26, and Luke 17:10 cannot bear, and it makes Paul contradict Romans 3:31 and Ephesians 2:10.
book_core_identification: 'Works' means deeds — actions performed — and is not a synonym for obedience. Obedience/disobedience names the deed's relation to a command: a work becomes obedience when it executes a legitimate command and disobedience when the deed or its commanding authority conflicts with God's command. Even complete obedience creates no wage-claim on God (duty, not debt); the Romans 4 contrast is faith versus labor presented for wages, not faith versus obedience.
book_secondary_elaborations: Romans 4:4-5 specifically pictures a laborer presenting work for wages, defining the excluded 'works' by their economic claim (debt) rather than by their moral content
James 2 presents Abraham's work as the visible enactment that perfects faith, not as a wage-claim
Luke 17:7-10 establishes that perfect obedience still leaves the Master owing nothing — duty vocabulary versus wage vocabulary

Paul's 'works of the law' occurrences do not carry one uniform referent; context decides whether God's law, the circumcision-party's demand, or an unnamed act is in view (developed in The End of the Law)
Works are 'commandment-shaped' (Ps 111:7; Rev 2:26) and thus can be kept; faith without works is dead because works are the enactment of trust
Ephesians 2:8-10 excludes works as purchase price while restoring them as the life the gift creates
strongest_counter_interpretation: The classical Lutheran/Reformed polemical reading in which 'works' — especially in Paul — intrinsically denotes human moral effort or obedience offered toward justification: 'to him that worketh' (Rom 4:4) means anyone attempting to obey God's law as a path to righteousness, so that faith is set against obedience-as-performance itself, and 'works' functions as shorthand for works-righteousness (Rom 4:4-5; 9:32; 11:6; Phil 3:9; Isa 64:6). On this reading the book's careful separation of 'work' (deed) from 'obedience' (relation to command) and from 'wage-claim' (economic posture) collapses: Paul's target is the obedient deed as such when relied upon.
counter_core_identification: Works are deeds understood as the outward expression and evidence of the inner spiritual condition — good works the fruit of faith and grace, evil works the fruit of the flesh — with the polemical Pauline usage treating 'works' as human obedience-effort opposed to grace in justification.
material_core_denial: To materially contradict the book, a counter would have to hold that 'works' is not deed-vocabulary at all but intrinsically encodes self-justifying obedience or moral effort, such that 'work' and 'obedience' are synonyms and Paul's polemic targets obedient deeds as such. This denial cannot survive the supplied texts: Psalm 111:7 predicates works of God Himself, Micah 6:16 uses 'works' for deeds executing Omri's evil statutes, Exodus 18:20 distinguishes the commanded work from the command, and Revelation 2:26 makes Christ's works something kept — none of which permits 'works' to mean self-righteous striving by definition without systematic equivocation.
counter_case: Romans 4:4-5, 9:32, 11:6, and Philippians 3:9 read naturally in a long exegetical tradition as opposing faith to law-obedience offered for justification, not merely to a wage-claim posture

Romans 3:28 and Galatians 2:16 set justification by faith against 'works of the law' generically, and Galatians 3:10 explicitly identifies God's own law, suggesting the deeds themselves — not only the manner of offering them — are excluded from justification
Isaiah 64:6 ('all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags') supports treating even obedient deeds as inadequate, blurring the book's deed/wage-claim distinction
The evidential-fruit framing (Matt 7:16-20; Eph 2:8-10; Jas 2:18) explains why works appear at judgment (Rev 20:12-13) without needing the book's command-execution taxonomy
book_explanatory_advantages: Micah 6:16 and Exodus 18:20 show 'works' as command-relative deed vocabulary on both the evil and good side — evil works are deeds keeping evil statutes — which the book's mechanism predicts and the works-as-effort reading cannot use

Luke 17:7-10 is directly explained: obedience is duty and creates no wage, so Paul's excluded 'him that worketh' (wage/debt vocabulary) is not the obedient servant; the counter must either ignore Luke 17:10 or make Jesus commend what Paul condemns

The book reconciles Romans 4:5 with Hebrews 11:8 and James 2:21-22 without contradiction: Abraham both 'believed' and 'obeyed' and was 'justified by works' as faith made visible — impossible if works-for-justification simply means obedience
Psalm 111:7 and Revelation 2:26 (God's works; 'keepeth my works') fit deed-vocabulary but embarrass any definition where 'works' intrinsically means human self-effort
Romans 3:31 ('we establish the law') and Ephesians 2:9-10 (not of works / created unto good works) are held together coherently: works excluded as purchase price, restored as created life

The distinction explains why identical outward deeds can be obedience or disobedience (Mark 7:9; Acts 5:29) depending on the commanding authority — a datum the evidential-fruit view leaves untheorized
counter_explanatory_advantages: The polemical reading has massive historical attestation and a simpler surface fit for Romans 4:4-5 and 11:6 read in isolation
It supplies a strong account of Philippians 3:9 and Isaiah 64:6, where even righteous performances are disclaimed
The evidential-fruit framing straightforwardly handles judgment-by-works texts (Rev 20:12-13) as works manifesting the heart
decisive_sources: Micah 6:16 — 'the statutes of Omri are kept, and all the works of the house of Ahab': works as deeds executing a commanding authority's statutes, the book's mechanism stated in the Old Testament's own grammar
Exodus 18:20 — ordinances taught, a way walked, 'the work that they must do': work defined as the deed distinct from the command at the law's first teaching
Luke 17:7-10 — complete obedience is duty and earns no wage, severing obedience from the wage-claim Paul excludes in Romans 4:4
Romans 4:4-5 — the excluded 'work' is defined by its economic claim (reward reckoned of debt), matching the laborer picture rather than obedience as such
James 2:21-22 with Hebrews 11:8 — Abraham's obedient work perfects faith rather than competing with it, coherent only if works ≠ wage-claim
Psalm 111:7 and Revelation 2:26 — works predicated of God and works that are 'kept', ruling out any definition in which works intrinsically mean self-justifying human effort
unresolved_objections: Mainstream exegesis of Romans 4:4 disputes that 'him that worketh' is restricted to the wage-labor posture; many read it as anyone performing deeds toward justification, and the entry's brief treatment does not fully adjudicate Romans 9:32/11:6/Philippians 3:9 within the printed texts

The strict terminological separation of 'work' (deed) from 'obedience' (relation) is a systematizing definition; NT usage is not uniformly this tidy (e.g., 'obedience of faith', Rom 1:5), so the book's taxonomy is a reconstruction rather than an explicit biblical lexicon entry

The entry's cross-reference to The End of the Law imports broader claims about the law's continuing normativity (e.g., readings of Colossians 2:16 and Galatians 4:8-10) that exceed what this entry's own citations establish and remain contested

Isaiah 64:6 and Philippians 3:9, cited by the counter, are not addressed in the supplied bundle, leaving one strand of the works-righteousness reading unanswered though not shown to contradict the core
